idea: Mercator's distortion drawn as data: Natural Earth continents each overlaid with Tissot's indicatrix circles, which balloon toward the poles, captioned 'Greenland is not the size of Africa.' Black ink on white; for people who have always suspected the map was lying.

A single rhumb line (loxodrome) spiralling forever toward the North Pole, computed and drawn in an orthographic view, captioned 'Constant bearing. Never arrives.' A navigator's version of stubbornness.

London to Tokyo as two paths on a flat Natural Earth map: the straight rhumb line and the curved great circle bowing north over Siberia, labelled 'Shortest' on the curve and 'Straightest' on the line. A quiet joke about the difference.

White on black: a Gauss-style triangulation net of the British Isles, thousands of survey triangles computed from a coastline, with the base line marked and the caption 'Everything measured from one ruler.' Appeals to surveying nerds.

Magnetic declination lines (isogons) of the world drawn from the public World Magnetic Model, the agonic line thickened, captioned 'North moves. Check the date.' Beautiful flowing contours with a practical warning.

Joy Division-style stacked ridgelines of the Alps built from public SRTM elevation data, each row offset and hidden-line removed, with only the small caption 'Matterhorn, 4478 m' marking the one peak.
Contour map of a perfectly invented island generated from noise, with soundings, compass rose and the line 'Here be nothing in particular.' Looks like a real chart until you read it.
The Voronoi diagram of the world's airports, each cell the territory closest to one runway, no coastlines drawn, so the continents appear only as cell density. Caption: 'Nearest way out.'

Harrison's longitude problem as a plot: a chart of a ship's position error growing at one degree of longitude per four minutes of clock drift, drawn as a fan of wandering dead-reckoning tracks that diverge across the Atlantic. Caption: 'Four minutes of clock error is sixty nautical miles of wrong.'

A Dymaxion-like icosahedral unfolding of the Natural Earth coastlines, the net laid out as a flat sheet with fold lines dashed, captioned 'Cut along the coast.' for people who like to see how the globe gets flattened.

Every map projection's Tissot error compared in a 3x3 grid of tiny globes (Mercator, Mollweide, Robinson, Peters and others), each captioned only with its name, and a bottom line 'No flat map is right.' A collector's chart.

Eratosthenes at Syene and Alexandria rendered as geometry: two sticks, two shadows, 7.2 degrees, and the computed arc around a circle, captioned '5,000 stadia and a shadow.' The first measurement of the Earth, as a clean line diagram.

Every ship track of the 1872 to 1876 Challenger expedition is not public as data, so instead: ocean-depth contours of the Mariana Trench from open bathymetry, shown as concentric rings fading to the deepest point, captioned 'Challenger Deep, 10,935 m. Still the lowest.'
A world map made of nothing but place names set in type at their coordinates, sized by latitude spacing so coastlines emerge from the words, with oceans left empty. Caption: 'The world, spelled out.'

Polar azimuthal equidistant map centred on the shirt wearer's likely home, Bern in Switzerland, here shown centred on Null Island (0,0) with distance rings every 2,000 km, captioned 'Null Island: the place where all your broken coordinates end up.' A geeky GIS joke.
Great-circle arcs between the 50 busiest city pairs drawn as glowing white curves on a black tee with no coastline at all, the world's shape emerging from travel. Caption: 'Drawn by where we go.'

Spherical triangle with angles summing to 270 degrees: one octant of the globe from the equator to the pole, drawn with its three right angles, captioned 'Three right angles. One triangle.' A navigator's proof, pleasingly paradoxical.
The sun's analemma plotted from real ephemeris data as a figure eight, with solstice and equinox dates marked, captioned 'Noon is not the same noon.' Sundial navigators and clock people will get it.

A seafloor of lost bearings: a compass rose built from 32 points, each line's length proportional to how often that wind direction blows in the North Atlantic from public wind data, so the rose becomes a lopsided star. Caption: 'Prevailing.'

The Swiss-style hachure map reborn: Mount Everest's SRTM terrain drawn only as slope lines (hachures) that follow steepest descent, white on black, with a single line of type 'Chomolungma. 8,849 m. Measured from 1855 triangulation, and nearly right.'
